slides.title: Quotient Laws of Exponents
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q4 is the move the whole lesson runs on: cancel a factor of 5 from top and bottom, and one 5 is left. A board showing 125/25 unsimplified has the arithmetic and not the idea.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Expand 5⁶ over 5³, cancel three pairs, three 5s remain. Then the rule. Ask why the base must be nonzero (division by zero) and why the bases must match (nothing cancels in 5⁶/2³).
OFF: 'Subtract, do not divide. 5⁶ over 5³ is 5³, not 5².' Question 6 in the round has 4⁴ waiting for the divider.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: Three copies of 8/10, multiplied: 8·8·8 over 10·10·10. The reveal on the line is the law. The task 'apply the law, do not simplify' exists because students want to reduce 8/10 first — both routes are right and give 0.512, and that is worth saying once.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Road 1: the pattern table, each column divided by the base. Road 2: 2³/2³ is 1 because anything nonzero over itself is 1, and it is 2⁰ by the quotient law — so 2⁰ = 1. The misconception is a⁰ = 0; the table kills it because the next entry after 2 is 2 ÷ 2, not 2 − 2.
OFF: 'Zero exponent means NO factors of the base are multiplied in. What is left is the 1 you always start from.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Same base? Yes, (−2). Which law? Then ask what the sign of the answer will be before anyone computes.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: Subtract, keep the base with its sign, evaluate: three negative factors, negative answer. The check row divides 64 by −8. A student who gets +8 dropped the sign at the last step.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches a divider (3³ = 27 from 6 ÷ 2) and a student who wrote 1⁴ by dividing the bases. 81 or 3⁴ is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.sub: A decimal base inside a quotient.
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Two routes: apply the power of a quotient, or divide first (0.2 ÷ 10 = 0.02) and raise that. Ask which they would choose and why.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: Route 1 keeps the numbers small until the last step. Route 2 is one power of a small decimal; a calculator gives 0.00000016 either way. Count the decimal places on the board: 0.0016 has four, 10⁴ moves four more.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: Catches a student who cubes only the numerator (27/4) or only the denominator (3/64). 27/64 is right; 0.421875 is the same value and also right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Quotient of powers, plain case. A board with 10⁸ added; 1² divided the bases.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 1 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Ruling 22's board: the running time is there to be read past. 8⁴ ÷ 8 = 4096 ÷ 8 = 512 is the check. A board with 4096 ignored the denominator; 8⁴ ÷ 1 is the same slip.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 2 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: One factor left, with its sign. A board with 6 dropped the sign; a board with 1 divided the bases.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 3 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: A rewrite, not a value. A board with (−5)⁷/10 applied the exponent to the numerator only; a board with −5⁷/10⁷ has lost the parentheses (same value here, but insist on them — the sign matters in 3.04).

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 4 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. A board full of B is the classic; send them back to the pattern table on Notes III — 2, then 2 ÷ 2.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 5 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Diagnostic. B is the one to watch: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 looks like the law. The expansion on Notes I is the answer — count what cancels.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 6 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Decimal base. A board with 0.5⁸ ÷ 0.5⁵ typed into a calculator gets 0.125 too — fine, but ask for the single power.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 7 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: The fraction is a distraction; the exponent decides. A board with 10/11 confused zero with the identity exponent.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 8 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.sub: Take your time. Boards up when you have written it.
slides.note: Written. The point is not 'both'; the point is the sentence 'so 2⁰ = 1'. A student who writes 'Hannah, because 2⁰ = 0' has the misconception in writing, which is the best place to find it.

slides.title: Whiteboards   ·   Question 9 of 9
slides.note: Reveal. Scan the back row first; question the blank boards before the wrong ones.

slides.title: Independent Set
slides.sub: Six questions. On your own, in silence.
slides.note: Hand out the Independent Set. Silent work. Circulate and mark what you see; do not teach. Whatever is not finished goes home.
